explanations.explanation: Close, friend, because mountains in a courtroom sound like a case against the whole world. But the text says, "For the LORD has a case against His people, and He will argue it against Israel…" (Micah 6:2). The mountains are called to hear it. The case is against Israel.

That's right. Micah 6:2 says, "For the LORD has a case against His people, and He will argue it against Israel…" The nations aren't in the dock at all. The mountains just get the front-row seats, and nobody asked them to bring cookies.

Yes! The LORD says, "Testify against Me how I have wearied you!" (Micah 6:3). He opens the floor and invites them to speak. I think that's a bold way to start a case, because He's the one asking the questions and still lets them answer.

explanations.answer: How they have kept His laws
explanations.explanation: I get why you went there, since a courtroom makes you think about rules. But the LORD doesn't ask them about their law-keeping here. He says, "Testify against Me how I have wearied you!" (Micah 6:3). The question is about what He has done to them, not what they've done.

explanations.answer: Who they trust more than Him
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but that isn't in these words. In this verse the LORD asks, "My people, what have I done to you?" and then says, "Testify against Me how I have wearied you!" (Micah 6:3). He opens the floor for them to speak against Him, and the text doesn't bring up anyone else they trust.

That's the trio! The LORD says, "I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam." (Micah 6:4). Moses was Israel's leader, Aaron was his brother, and Miriam was their sister (Numbers 26:59). Three siblings walking ahead of a whole nation, which is a lot of family road trip.

Those are real names with real stories, but they're not the ones in this verse. Micah 6:4 says, "I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam." Joshua and Caleb were two of the twelve spies sent into Canaan (Numbers 13:6, 8, 16), so you're in the right part of the Bible, friend. Just a different page.

Nice names, but this verse is about the Egypt story, and that's a different chapter of history. Micah 6:4 says, "I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam." Eli was a priest, Hannah was the woman who prayed for a son, and Samuel was the son she bore (1 Samuel 1:9, 20).

explanations.answer: So they'll see the LORD is righteous
explanations.explanation: You got it. The LORD says, "Remember your journey from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you may acknowledge the righteousness of the LORD." (Micah 6:5). Remembering is how they see it. I think that's why He keeps pointing them back to what He already did.

explanations.answer: So they'll keep far away from Moab
explanations.explanation: Moab does come up, since Balak was its king. But the verse doesn't say to stay away from anybody. It says, "Remember your journey from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you may acknowledge the righteousness of the LORD." (Micah 6:5). The point is seeing who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: So they'll never trust a foreign king
explanations.explanation: Balak was a foreign king, so I see the connection, friend. But the text never gives that as the reason. It says they should remember "…so that you may acknowledge the righteousness of the LORD." (Micah 6:5). The whole purpose is about the LORD, not about kings.

Yes! The first offering it wonders about is this: "Should I come to Him with burnt offerings, with year-old calves?" (Micah 6:6). That's where the shopping list starts, and it's about to get a lot bigger. Right after, it asks about "…thousands of rams…" and "…ten thousand rivers of oil?" (Micah 6:7).

Look again at the verse, friend. It asks, "Should I come to Him with burnt offerings, with year-old calves?" (Micah 6:6). The burnt offerings are the first thing mentioned, and the year-old calves come right with them.

I can see why the long list of offerings would make it feel that way. But the very next line says, "He has shown you, O man, what is good." (Micah 6:8). Nobody is left in the dark. After all those questions comes a clear answer.

That's right. After the questions about offerings, the passage says, "He has shown you, O man, what is good." (Micah 6:8). The good thing isn't a secret. It's already been shown, so nobody has to guess or keep adding to the pile.

explanations.answer: Justice and mercy and a humble walk with Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! "And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:8). Three things, and none of them need a shopping trip. I could stamp that on every cookie in the box.

explanations.answer: More and bigger offerings at every feast
explanations.explanation: That's the direction the questions in verses 6 and 7 were heading, friend. But verse 8 answers with something else: "And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?" The answer isn't more offerings. It's how to live.

explanations.answer: A long trip up to the temple every year
explanations.explanation: A big trip sounds like something a person would do to be serious about God. Verse 5 does mention a journey, from Shittim to Gilgal, but that's not what verse 8 says He requires. It says, "And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:8). Justice, mercy and a humble walk can start wherever you're standing.
